messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Four years ago, his son’s sudden septic shock had turned a quiet pediatric ward into a suffocating maze of beeping monitors and clinical staff. Dev had spent three days seated on a narrow cot beside a intubated boy, watching specialists adjust drips and turn valves while his son’s breathing grew erratic. The helplessness of that room, where a single misplaced wire or delayed alarm could be fatal, seared itself into his nervous system. Even now, at fifty, the crisp snap of latex gloves or the sterile, antiseptic tang of a waiting room sends a jolt straight to his ribs. When he or his wife steps into an examination room for a routine checkup, his pulse hammers against his collarbone, and he finds himself gripping the metal armrests until his knuckles whiten. The fear of being physically separated from his child’s bedside during a crisis now warps his nights; he refuses to sleep alone in their bedroom, insisting his wife take the guest room so he can keep the master door open and maintain a direct line of sight to the hall. Each time one of those visceral alarms rang off, Dev’s mind instantly deployed its familiar defensive routines. The antiseptic scent or the clinical examination directly fueled his worst-case rehearsal, his mental screen cycling through every possible way his son’s condition could collapse if a monitor failed or a dosage was miscalculated. To momentarily quiet the rising panic, he would call his wife or his primary care doctor, asking repeatedly if the current symptoms or test results meant his son was stable, needing their calm voices to anchor him. Simultaneously, a colder, sharper current of thought would take hold. He fixated on the attending physician as the assailant who had caused the crisis, convinced the man’s rushed dismissal was a deliberate failure of duty. Dev spent hours planning exactly how to get even, drafting detailed grievances about how he would hold that specific doctor accountable for the terror he had endured. Working as a digital animator, Dev usually found solace in the rhythmic flow of drawing software, but the pattern had begun to bleed into his studio. While rendering a complex scene of a character falling through a dark corridor, a faint whiff of cleaning spray from the janitorial cart triggered a familiar spike of dread. Instantly, his worst-case rehearsal took over; he stopped rendering, his cursor hovering as his mind fast-forwarded to his son’s hospital bed shaking, the ventilator alarms blaring, and his own hands trembling too much to hold the emergency call button. The anxiety demanded immediate relief, so he abandoned his workstation and paced the studio floor, dialing his wife’s number. “Just tell me again that the new cardiologist’s report is completely normal,” he pleaded, his voice tight. “I need to know he’s safe before I can sit back down.” His wife’s reassurance offered only a fleeting pause. Once the call ended, the relief evaporated, replaced once again by the cold, grinding focus on the attending physician. His mental rehearsals and his vengeful fixation directly intensified his reaction to sensory cues, ensuring that each subsequent hospital smell or medical procedure struck him with renewed intensity. Over the past fourteen months, this feedback loop had tightened into an inescapable rhythm. He stopped scheduling his own annual physicals, opting to push them off for months at a time. He began avoiding hospitals altogether, rerouting his drives to bypass urgent care centers and taking alternate highways that added forty minutes to his commute. What finally drove him to seek help this week was a moment at the studio when a simple file corruption caused him to break down sobbing, realizing he could no longer tolerate the silence of his own apartment or the weight of his son’s fragile health. He walked into the therapist’s office hoping to dismantle the exhausting cycle before it stole the last years of his son’s childhood from him, terrified that if he didn’t find a way to quiet the relentless predictions of catastrophe, he would never feel safe in his own life again.
